question_text:
A 39-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. He was diagnosed with latent tuberculosis infection 3 months ago. He has had generalized fatigue and dyspnea on exertion for the past 6 weeks. He does not smoke and drinks 2–3 beers on weekends. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows conjunctival pallor. Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 72 μm3
Red cell distribution width 17% (N = 13–15)
Reticulocyte count 0.7%
Leukocyte count 6,800/mm3
Platelet count 175,000/mm3
Serum
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Iron 246 μg/dL
Ferritin 446 ng/mL
Total iron-binding capacity 212 μg/dL (N = 250–450)
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?"?

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with microcytic anemia (low hemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL and low MCV of 72 μm3) and elevated ferritin (446 ng/mL) alongside low total iron-binding capacity (TIBC of 212 μg/dL). These findings are consistent with anemia of chronic disease (ACD), which is often seen in the context of chronic inflammation, such as that caused by latent tuberculosis infection. The high ferritin level indicates iron stores are adequate, which contradicts iron deficiency anemia. The low reticulocyte count (0.7%) further supports ACD, as it suggests inadequate bone marrow response to anemia. Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is chronic inflammation due to his latent tuberculosis infection.
